entities.summary: Henry IV of England, also known as Henry Bolingbroke, was the King of England from 1399 to 1413, Lord of Ireland, and Duke of Aquitaine. He was the son of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, and a grandson of King Edward III. Henry's ascension to the throne was marked by the overthrow of his cousin, King Richard II, who was deposed in 1399. This event, known as the 'Readeption of Richard II,' had significant consequences for the balance of power in medieval England. Henry's reign was also notable for the passage of the Statute of Pleading, which reformed the English legal system. The English Parliament, established during his reign, became a powerful institution that would shape the course of English history. Henry IV's legacy extends beyond his own reign, as his policies and decisions influenced the subsequent monarchs, including his son, King Henry V. The Black Death, which ravaged Europe during his reign, had a profound impact on English society, leading to significant social, economic, and cultural changes. The legacy of Henry IV can be seen in the continued relevance of the English Parliament and the ongoing impact of the Black Death on modern society. The fact that Henry IV was a grandson of King Edward III and a son of John of Gaunt makes him a crucial figure in the Plantagenet dynasty, which ruled England for over 300 years.
